episodes.211646: A line of heavy thunderstorms moved east through northwest Alabama shortly after daybreak. The storms produced gusty winds knocked down a few trees. The rainfall contributed to a pickup truck hydroplaning off of westbound U.S. Highway 72 and into Shoal Creek near the Shoal Creek bridge, killing the occupant.
episodes.211696: Severe thunderstorm activity occurred across southern portions of Central Alabama from the evening of May 6 into the overnight hours of May 7. Most of the severe weather occurred in the form of wind damage and hail from three distinct supercells across parts of Montgomery, Macon, Greene, Hale, and Sumter counties. Large hail, up to baseball size, was observed just east of downtown Montgomery and later near Forkland in Greene County. As training thunderstorms resulted in 3 to 5 inches of rain falling, several instances of flash flooding occurred in parts of Montgomery, Elmore, Autauga, Marengo, and Sumter counties.
episodes.212867: An approaching northern stream trough in combination with sufficient moisture resulted in the development of isolated high based convection across Utah on May 5th. This activity resulted in strong outflow wind gusts, and at least one instance of an isolated severe wind gust.
episodes.213174: A line of strong thunderstorms with gusty winds rolled east through southern middle Tennessee shortly after daybreak, downing a few trees.
episodes.213445: A slow moving cold front sagged southeast across the area sparking a broken line of thunderstorms that moved across eastern OH and northwestern PA in the evening hours. A narrow axis of 100-250 J/kg of MLCAPE and 30 knots of effective shear supported a localized damaging wind threat resulting in power poles and trees down.
episodes.213446: A slow moving cold front sagged southeast across the area sparking a broken line of thunderstorms that moved across eastern OH and northwestern PA in the evening hours. A narrow axis of 100-250 J/kg of MLCAPE and 30 knots of effective shear supported a localized damaging wind threat resulting in power poles and trees down.
episodes.213557: A line of storms approached the Mississippi River, posing primarily a damaging wind threat. However, given the timing of the line crossing the area, the flash flooding risk heightened. Storms trained as a frontal boundary sunk south. A majority of the region experienced heavy rainfall the day prior during the morning hours, additional rains from this system continued to agitate rivers and streams. A storm trained right over the Memphis Metro resulting in flash flooding.
episodes.213657: A significant severe weather outbreak occurred across northeast Louisiana and central and southern MS amid a favorably sheared environment. A capping inversion limited early convection, which allowed for higher instability. Supercell initiation began in the afternoon and eroded the capping inversion to allow a long track supercell to take root. This supercell produced a long track EF-3 tornados. Several  other brief, weak tornadoes occurred. Supercells also produced hail as large as baseballs and straight line wind damage also occurred. The duration of rainfall also lead to flash flooding.
episodes.213660: A significant severe weather outbreak across northeast Louisiana and central and southern MS amid a favorably sheared environment. A capping inversion limited early convection, which allowed for higher instability. Supercell initiation began in the afternoon and eroded the capping inversion to allow a long track supercell to take root. This supercell produced a long track EF-3 tornados. Several other brief, weak tornadoes occurred. Supercells also produced hail as large as baseballs and straight line wind damage also occurred. The duration of rainfall also lead to flash flooding.
episodes.213817: A slowly advancing cold front was positioned beneath strong west-southwesterly flow downstream of a broad upper-level trough with embedded shortwaves. A moist low level layer and strong instability combined with strengthening deep-layer and low-level wind shear to support discrete supercells across southwest and southern Mississippi during the late afternoon and evening. These storms produced large hail and multiple tornadoes over southwest Mississippi, one EF1 and one EF2 tornado.
episodes.213953: Thunderstorms developed along a cold front that moved through South-Central Texas. Some of these storms produced large hail.
episodes.213964: The 2026 spring breakup along the Yukon River was highly dynamic, defined by a combination of thermal ice decay and severe mechanical ice jams. Because of an exceptionally cold winter and a cool spring, the river ice was thicker than normal and had not deteriorated significantly before the main breakup front arrived. Early-season flooding was driven by localized snowmelt and ice jams on independent river systems and upper sections of the Yukon River.
episodes.214028: The combination of multiple frontal boundaries draped across central Arkansas in cohesion with approaching H500 troughs led to an atmosphere that was conducive for the development of multiple storms across the state. The majority of these isolated storms would remain strong, but a few managed to become severe producing a few instances of severe wind gusts and large hail. Additionally, as cold air aloft remained increasingly cold and air at the surface became increasingly hot multiple cold air funnels were noted with a few strong thunderstorms across the state.
episodes.214063: A few severe thunderstorms produced large hail across the Northwest Hill Country.
episodes.214075: A cold front stalled across the region while multiple short waves moved overhead. This produce multiple days of unsettled weather.

Yukon river ice stopped moving and jammed near Eagle, forcing water levels to rise rapidly upstream. Water approached road levels between the town and the village, and large blocks of river ice were pushed onshore. Local residents and official NWS River Watch flights confirmed that water was affecting road access into Eagle Village.
The I-80 at MP 40 Knolls mesonet station recorded a wind gust of 62 mph as a result of outflow winds associated with a nearby cluster of showers and thunderstorms moving through the area.

A NWS ground survey confirmed an EF-1 tornado with maximum sustained winds of 90 mph tracked across portions of southeast Pike. This tornado began near Smithburg, MS at the intersection of Mount Herman Road Silver Drive where it uprooted a tree and snapped branches. Additional EF-0 tree damage was identified on Blanchard and Smithburg roads. The tornado peaked in intensity as an EF-1 as it crossed over Harold Alford Road uprooting and snapping several trees as well as taking down wooden transmission lines. At this point, the tornado exited Pike County and entered Walthall County.
Several trees were snapped and uprooted in the Bloomo Community.

A NWS ground survey confirmed an EF-1 tornado with maximum sustained winds of 90 mph tracked across portions of southeast Pike County and entered Walthall County near Harold Alford Road. It was  uprooting and snapping several trees as well as taking down wooden transmission lines as it traversed this area. The tornado then weakened caused EF-0 damage to trees as it crossed Brockdale Rd and the Bogue Chitto River. The end point of this tornado is estimated to be after it crossed MS Hwy 27 after it caused additional tree damage in a confluent pattern.

A swath of large hail ranging from golf ball to baseball size fell across Neshoba County and Kemper County, roughly along south of the MS Highway 16 corridor. This corridor stretched from southwest of Philadelphia to De Kalb.

Flash flooding occurred in downtown Montgomery following heavy rainfall. Numerous streets were flooded, also affecting some buildings. Specific reports of flooding that were received included the Alabama State Capitol building, Atlanta Highway near Eastern Blvd, and along Perry Hill Rd.
Multiple trees were blown down across Lawrence County.

Over the course of two hours and nine minutes, a strong, long|track tornado trekked 81.9 miles across South Mississippi. It|began in southwestern Adams County, then moved across northern|Wilkinson, southeastern Adams, southern Franklin, and central|Lincoln counties, before lifting on the south side of Monticello|in Lawrence County. The tornado intensity peaked at a high-end EF3|with an estimated maximum wind of 160 MPH just east of Garden|City in southwestern Franklin County. The maximum path width was|1.5 miles in east central Lincoln County.||The tornado began in the St. Catherine Creek National Wildlife|Refuge in southwestern Adams County, causing sporadic tree damage|as it crossed US Hwy 61, Will Washington Rd, and the Homochitto|River into northern Wilkinson County. The path straddled the|Wilkinson and Adams County line for 7-8 miles, remaining mainly on|the Wilkinson County side, but producing damage on the Adams County|side at times as it strengthened. The tornado then fully re-|entered the southeasternmost corner of Adams County, producing|heavy timber damage over a 3/4 to 1 mile wide footprint as it|entered the Homochitto National Forest for the first time. Here, a|few swaths of tree damage began to reach EF2 thresholds.||Crossing into southwestern Franklin County, heavy timber damage,|reaching EF2 intensity at times, continued into the Garden City|community. A few structures were impacted in this area, including|multiple buildings with roof damage, a mobile home that was|destroyed, and multiple outbuildings that were destroyed. The|tornado reached its peak intensity as it continued east-|northeastward and reentered the Homochitto National Forest. As it|crossed Freewood Road, it intensified, snapping a high percentage|of trees through dense pine forest and mixed forest tracts. While|tree damage was extensive in this area, ground surveys revealed|there were numerous dead snags throughout this section of the|forest, possibly impacted by prior drought, fire, or some|combination thereof. As a result, it was determined that several|of the trees along the damage path originally believed to be|debarked by the tornado were already without bark or had bark that|was easily stripped. Still, extensive damage to the healthy trees|through this portion of southwestern Franklin County warranted a|high end EF3 rating. The tornado remained strong as it crossed|Bunkley Road twice, then weakened slightly as it crossed the|Homochitto River. It continued producing periodic EF2 damage east|of Gloster Road and as it crossed US Highway 98 near Okhissa Lake,|where the nearby Bude RAWS site recorded a 76 mph gust on the|south side of the track. East of the lake, the tornado weakened|further to EF0-EF1 intensity, leaving patches of downed trees|across Berrytown, Bogue Chitto, Burt Jordan, Murray, and Olympia|Roads before moving into western Lincoln County.||The tornado began to intensify again as it passed near the West|Lincoln community, producing EF2 damage as it crossed West Lincoln|Drive and briefly reaching EF3 intensity just east of that|location, bodily removing two trees and moving them 5 to 10 yards.|There was also a large portion of a snapped pine was thrown about|30 to 40 yards into a field in the same location. As the tornado|approached Jackson Liberty Road, the tornado collapsed a lattice|electrical transmission tower and removed the top half of another.|Along Auburn Drive, multiple mobile homes were destroyed, two|houses sustained major roof loss, and two vehicles were moved. The|tornado then crossed Calvary Drive, Apple Trail, and Pecan Lane,|causing widespread timber loss and further structural roof damage.|After crossing I-55, the storm reached low-end EF3 strength near|Stoneybrook Trail, where a home suffered exterior wall failure and|extensive tree damage and some tree debarking was observed.|Crossing US Highway 51, the tornado swept directly through a|mobile home park, destroying 10 to 20 mobile homes and tossing|several vehicles. Additional mobile homes were destroyed just east|of Highway 51 north of Hog Chain Drive, with severe tree damage|persisting near the Bogue Chitto River.||Pushing into eastern Lincoln County, the circulation widened|significantly expanding up to 1.5 miles wide east of Pricedale|Drive. Widespread EF2 damage continued across Pricedale Drive and|Mount Olive Road, with the tornado destroying a mobile home,|heavily damaging several houses, and impacting multiple farm|buildings. At a destroyed hay shed, a single hay bale was moved 10|to 20 yards toward the center of the path. Near the Enterprise|community, tree damage spiked once more, and several homes|suffered major roof damage across MS Highway 583, Mallalieu Drive,|and surrounding roads. After crossing East Lincoln Road near|Wellman Drive, the tornado tracked east-northeastward toward|Harmony. Along Harmony Drive, it destroyed multiple chicken houses|and damaged several homes. Severe timber damage including partial|debarking continued east of Pleasant Grove Drive as the tornado|approached the Lawrence County line.||The tornado maintained EF2 intensity into western Lawrence|County, with significant damage to timber continuing across Trace|Road and Ford Calcote Road. In this area, a barn and mobile home|were demolished. Another home sustained heavy roof damage as the|tornado paralleled Lower Brookhaven Road. It then began to weaken|as it crossed Carmel Road and Carmel New Hope Road, then lifted on|the south side of Monticello, just east of MS Highway 27 near|Halls Creek.
A swath of large hail fell across northern Jefferson Davis County with hailstones ranging from golf ball size to greater than 2 inches in diameter.

This summary covers primarily the Wilkinson County, MS portion of the track. For more information regarding this tornado please refer to WFO Jackson, MS's public information statements. The damage path of a large and significant tornado began between E Sibley Farms Rd and US Hwy 61 in Adams County, MS. Gray Sky/Vexcel and Sentinel-2 high-resolution satellite imagery was heavily leveraged over this rural and inaccessible portion of the track. The tornado produced occasional swaths of defined EF-1 tree damage as it moved into Wilkinson County along the Homochitto River and the damage path became apparently much larger and more multi-vortex in nature with several swaths of damage noted from vortices along and south of the mean path. The sheer amount of tree damage that extended over a half mile south of the mean track made it difficult to differentiate between RFD and subtornadic vortex damage, but the ingestion of this vorticity clearly assisted in rapid intensification of this tornado beyond Possum Corner, MS. An increasingly intense and large swath of downed trees began near Possum Corner Road, south of the Homochitto River. Widespread deforestation became increasingly evident as the tornado tracked east-northeast with several swaths of greater than 80% deforestation rated EF-2 for widespread snapped trunks of pine and mixed forest. The lack of well-built structures in the path of this tornado limited sampling of the peak rating of this tornado. As the tornado approached Doloroso-Rosetta Rd and the Homochitto River, the treefall pattern became cyclonic in orientation and indicative of a potential change of direction which is supported by Climavision V018 data from St. Francisville, LA. Near Old Hwy 61 Road and Perry Town Rd, barn and outbuilding structures were heavily damaged or destroyed. Almost all trees were snapped. High resolution satellite imagery also denoted numerous confluent swaths of damaging feeding into the main track from the south, indicative of subtornadic vortices and potentially a satellite tornado as it neared Old Hwy 61 Road. The tornado reached an initial peak width of 1200 yards here incorporating these feeder vortices. The tornado then continued east causing additional swaths of tree damage north of Perry Town Road before crossing the Homochitto River and back into Adams County. This tornado was continuously on the ground for approximately 81.9 miles over the span of 2 hours and 9 minutes through Adams, Wilkinson, Franklin, and Lincoln counties before concluding southwest of Monticello, MS in Lawrence County. This tornado peaked as an EF-3 east of Garden City, MS as well as near Thayer, MS in NWS Jackson's area of responsibility.

This tornado began near or just west of the intersections of Tatum Salt Dome Road and R Thompson Road where it produced damage to trees crossing Tatum Salt Dome Road with a narrow swath of damage produced just north of R Thompson Rd. The tornado moved eastward through the Half Moon Creek lower wooded areas before crossing Beach Road, retaining a consolidated core that could be observed transecting the roadway twice as the tornado track roughly paralleled the roadway. The tornado produced mostly vegetative damage until it approached western Purvis in the Boggy Hollow areas where outbuildings were damaged or destroyed and trees were blown onto homes. A mobile home was blown off of its blocks just north of Purvis-to-Columbia Road, which the tornado approximately moved along as it traveled east-northeast. The tornado intensified to its maximum intensity, producing damage that suggests maximum winds were at least 135 mph as several residences had roofs removed as well as some exterior walls blown inward near Coal Town Road and Highway 589. Significant damage was also observed along Central Industrial Row where several metal building system (MBS) warehouse and commercial buildings had walls and internal structures including pillars/columns and roofing purlins destroyed. Numerous other facilities suffered substantial loss of roofing materials including the Lamar County Multi-Purpose Center. The tornado continued eastward downing numerous trees and causing widespread damage to roofs and outbuildings before dissipating just east of US Highway 11. The tornado at maximum width was estimated at 600 yards, had a track length of 13.4 miles, and had a maximum estimated intensity of 135 mph, EF-2.
